chunks: "Both stop reflections, but at different ends. Series termination is a resistor at the driver so that the driver plus the resistor equals the line impedance.
The driver launches only half the step into the line, at the open far end the wave doubles to full amplitude, and the reflection returns to the source where it's absorbed.
So there's no ringing, no DC power, just one resistor.
But the line sees a half-height step for a round trip, so any receiver in the middle sees a staircase and a wrong or late switch.
Only the receiver at the very end sees a clean edge. Parallel termination is a resistor equal to Z0 at the end of the line.
The wave arrives full amplitude and is absorbed, so every receiver along the line sees a clean full step on the first pass.
The costs: the driver now sees a DC load, so power is real, 3.
3 volts into 50 ohms is 66 milliamps, and the high level drops because the driver and the resistor form a divider; Thevenin, VTT and AC variants reduce that.
So: point-to-point, power-sensitive: series. Multi-drop buses or when the signal must be clean along the line, or high-speed differential links: parallel at the end.
And I'll often use series for clocks because it also slows the edge a little and helps EMI."
